latin.forms: praeceps, praecipitis; comparative praecipitior; superlative praecipitissimus. Genitive praecipitis shows the stem praециpit-. Neuter praeceps often used substantively for 'precipice, steep place.'
latin.etymology: From prae ('before, forward') + caput ('head'), literally 'head-foremost.' The compound suggests falling or rushing with the head first. Gives rise to praecipitō ('to throw headlong, hurry').
latin.literary_context: Virgil uses praeceps repeatedly in the Aeneid to describe violent motion and passion. In Book 2, Aeneas describes Troy's fall: 'urbs antiqua ruit multos dominata per annos; / plurima perque vias sternuntur inertia passim / corpora perque domos et religiosa deorum / limina' — the city rushes praeceps to destruction.
latin.usage_example: In praeceps ac pronum corruere omnia. — Everything rushed headlong into ruin.
latin.did_you_know: Cicero favored praeceps for describing both physical precipices and metaphorical hasty decisions. The phrase 'se praecipitem dare' (to throw oneself headlong) became proverbial for extreme rashness, while the neuter 'in praeceps' (into the abyss) appears throughout historical writing to mark irreversible catastrophe.

greek.forms: nom. δίκη, gen. δίκης, dat. δίκῃ, acc. δίκην; plural δίκαι, δικῶν, δίκαις, δίκας
greek.etymology: From Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (to show, point out). Related to δείκνυμι (to show) and Latin dicere (to say). The root sense involves pointing out what is right or proper.
greek.literary_context: Hesiod in Works and Days presents Δίκη as a personified goddess, daughter of Zeus, who reports human injustices to her father. Aeschylus makes δίκη central to the Oresteia trilogy, where competing claims of justice drive the entire action until Athena establishes a court to replace blood vengeance.
greek.usage_example: Ζεὺς δ᾽ ἐπιτέλλει δίκην βροτοῖσιν. — Zeus appoints justice for mortals.
greek.did_you_know: The personification of Δίκη as a goddess represents the Greek understanding that justice is not merely human convention but a cosmic principle enforced by Zeus himself. Our word deictic (pointing out) shares the same Indo-European root.

french.etymology: From Latin chimaera, from Greek χίμαιρα (khimaira), originally a mythological fire-breathing monster, later extended to mean any fantastic or impossible conception.
french.literary_context: Nerval uses chimère in his sonnet "El Desdichado" from Les Chimères (1854): the title of the collection itself suggests impossible dreams and mythic hybridities that haunt the poet's quest for lost love and identity.
french.usage_example: Il poursuit des chimères au lieu de vivre dans le réel. — He pursues illusions instead of living in reality.
french.did_you_know: The plural form chimères became the title of Gérard de Nerval's final collection of sonnets, where the word evokes both the mythological monsters of antiquity and the hallucinatory visions that characterized his visionary poetics and descent into madness.

german.forms: die Zerrissenheit (nom.), der Zerrissenheit (gen./dat.), die Zerrissenheit (acc.); no plural in this sense
german.etymology: From zerrissen (past participle of zerreißen 'to tear apart') + -heit (nominal suffix). Root reißen from Old High German rīzan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wrītaną.
german.literary_context: Heinrich Heine used Zerrissenheit to describe the divided consciousness of the modern intellectual caught between reason and feeling, romantic longing and Enlightenment skepticism. The concept pervades Goethe's Die Leiden des jungen Werthers, where the protagonist embodies this fundamental inner split.
german.usage_example: Die Zerrissenheit seiner Seele trieb ihn zur Verzweiflung. — The division of his soul drove him to despair.
german.did_you_know: Zerrissenheit became a key term for the Young Germany movement in the 1830s, describing the predicament of a generation torn between political idealism and the constraints of Metternich's conservative order. Hegel addressed this condition philosophically as the unhappy consciousness (das unglückliche Bewußtsein) split against itself.

oldenglish.forms: nominative sg. brimhengest; genitive brimhengstes; nominative pl. brimhengstas; genitive pl. brimhengesta
oldenglish.etymology: Compound of brim ('sea, surf, water') + hengest ('horse, stallion'). The kenning transforms a ship into a steed that rides the waves, a characteristic device of Germanic heroic poetry.
oldenglish.literary_context: This kenning appears in Beowulf during the hero's sea voyage to Denmark, where the poet describes the warriors' ship as a brimhengest cutting through ocean swells with its curved prow.
oldenglish.usage_example: Gewat þa ofer wægholm brimhengest faran, flota famigheals. — Then the sea-horse departed over the water, the foamy-necked floater.
oldenglish.did_you_know: Anglo-Saxon poets created elaborate kennings by combining concrete nouns to describe ships: besides brimhengest they used sæhengest (sea-horse), wægflota (wave-floater), and sundwudu (sea-wood), each metaphor revealing how the Germanic imagination saw vessels as living creatures or natural extensions of their element.
